forces.title: Rising network charges boost T&D utility regulated revenue
forces.description: Network charges for energy infrastructure, including gas transmission and distribution, have increased by 25% over the last 18 months, significantly exceeding inflation. This trend provides a tailwind for regulated gas T&D utilities as it translates into a growing regulated asset base (RAB) and associated tariff revenues, supporting investment recovery. However, it exacerbates affordability concerns for households and increases pressure on the overall energy price cap.

forces.title: Elevated wholesale gas prices increase price cap pressure
forces.description: Higher wholesale gas prices, influenced by global energy markets and geopolitical events, directly increase the cost of energy for retail suppliers. This puts upward pressure on the overall energy price cap, leading to increased consumer bills. While Gas T&D Utilities do not own the commodity, the resulting affordability concerns and the regulatory response to rising consumer costs can indirectly impact their operating environment and future tariff negotiations and approvals.

forces.title: Declining natural gas demand a structural headwind
forces.description: European natural gas demand is projected to decrease by 2% annually until 2030, and further decline through 2040. This structural trend represents a significant headwind for Gas Transmission & Distribution Utilities, impacting asset utilization and long-term revenue prospects. It necessitates strategic shifts, potentially requiring these regulated entities to adapt their infrastructure for new energy vectors or diversify into electricity-related activities to maintain viability.
forces.source_title: Utilities at an inflection point: Four strategic evolutions ahead

forces.title: Policies target natural gas reliance in heating sector
forces.description: Energy sovereignty efforts are extending to the heating and cooling sector, which heavily relies on natural gas. The European Commission's 2026 Heating and Cooling Strategy aims to support local heat planning, district heating modernization, and renewable heat sources. These policies directly seek to reduce dependence on fossil fuels for heating, representing a significant structural headwind for Gas Transmission & Distribution Utilities, whose core business includes gas supply to households and small commercial customers for heating.
forces.source_title: Utilities at an inflection point: Four strategic evolutions ahead

forces.title: Geopolitical events increase energy supply and price risks
forces.description: Disruptions in global energy chokepoints, such as the Strait of Hormuz in 2026, quickly translate into supply and price risks for energy commodities. While Gas Transmission & Distribution Utilities do not own the gas commodity, such events raise the strategic value of domestic and diversified energy supply and contribute to wholesale price volatility. This environment can lead to increased regulatory intervention to manage affordability and security of supply, indirectly impacting operational frameworks for regulated gas networks.
forces.source_title: Utilities at an inflection point: Four strategic evolutions ahead

forces.title: Substantial capital flowing into regulated network assets
forces.description: European utilities, including major UK players like National Grid and SSE, allocated significant capital to regulated network assets in 2025. National Grid reported a total network Regulated Asset Base (RAB) of EUR 51 billion for FY2025, with 30% attributed to gas networks. This sustained investment indicates a strong and growing revenue base for Gas Transmission & Distribution Utilities, supported by predictable, regulated returns and long-duration capital deployment.
forces.source_title: Utilities at an inflection point: Four strategic evolutions ahead

forces.title: Ofgem price cap hikes support utility cost recovery
forces.description: Ofgem's utility price cap is set to increase in July and September 2026, delaying the reduction of energy inflation. For Gas Transmission & Distribution Utilities, these hikes allow for the recovery of rising operating and network costs under a regulated tariff model, contributing to revenue stability. However, they also expose households to persistent high energy bills, potentially increasing political and regulatory pressure on the sector to manage affordability in the near term.
forces.source_title: Q3 UK economic outlook: Growth holds, inflation bites

viewpoints.title: Balancing essential network investment with household energy affordability is challenging
viewpoints.description: The UK faces a period requiring substantial investment in energy networks and infrastructure, including gas transmission and distribution. While these investments are crucial for modernization and system resilience, they lead to increased network costs, significantly outpacing inflation. Policymakers are challenged to balance the need for infrastructure upgrades with consumer expectations for affordable, stable energy bills. This creates a difficult operating environment for regulated Gas T&D Utilities, potentially leading to increased scrutiny and pressure on tariff structures.

viewpoints.title: Shrinking natural gas demand drives diversification for European gas utilities
viewpoints.description: European natural gas demand is projected to decline by an average of 2% annually until 2030, with further decreases expected through 2040. This structural shift necessitates that historical gas utilities, including Gas Transmission & Distribution providers, explore expansion into power value chain activities and other energy solutions. The contraction in core demand segments poses a significant strategic challenge, compelling a re-evaluation of asset utilization and long-term business models for regulated gas infrastructure.
viewpoints.source_title: Utilities at an inflection point: Four strategic evolutions ahead

viewpoints.title: Ofgem price cap hikes delay energy inflation pullback, increase borrowing costs
viewpoints.description: Ofgem's utility price cap hikes, scheduled for July and September 2026, are expected to delay the reduction of energy inflation in the UK. This creates a challenging environment for consumers and businesses, who will face persistent inflation and higher borrowing costs. For Gas Transmission & Distribution Utilities, while cap adjustments allow for cost recovery, the broader economic context of sticky inflation and elevated interest rates increases the cost of financing capital-intensive infrastructure projects.
viewpoints.source_title: Q3 UK economic outlook: Growth holds, inflation bites

demand_drivers.description: Increasing electricity share of final energy consumption is displacing natural gas demand.
Deployment of heat pumps for residential heating reduces reliance on natural gas.
Industrial processes are increasingly shifting from gas to electricity for energy needs.

market_sizing.methodology: Projection of European natural gas demand (EU-27 plus Norway, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom) in thousand terawatt-hours, converted from billion cubic meters. The decline is projected based on McKinsey's Global Energy Perspective 2025. Additionally, Regulated Asset Base (RAB) figures for UK utilities are provided.
